topic: What if you were stuck on Mars?
title: WHAT IF YOU WERE
STUCK ON MARS?

power.rule: you can dig water, make air and stretch power out of a dead planet — but you can't leave it
power.look: the habitat's own instruments: a filling gauge, a lit console, a storm on the window

script.text: No water. Dig. Ice under the dirt. Melt it.
No air. The machine splits carbon dioxide. Breathe.

script.beat: 1 cold open, demo 3 (the planet pushes back)
script.text: Dust buries the solar panels. Sweep. Lights on.
What if you were stuck on Mars?

script.beat: 4 the turn: the cost, one real fact
script.text: One catch: rescue waits for the planets to line up. Every twenty-six months. That's real.
The next window opens tomorrow. Maybe.

science.claim: Rescue waits for the planets to line up. Every twenty-six months.
science.working: A return flight launches when Earth and Mars are aligned for the cheapest path (a Hohmann transfer window); these repeat with the planets' synodic period: 779.9 days, about 25.9 months, so one launch window every 26 months. A crew stranded after a departure has to survive through the next window roughly every two years.
science.source: NASA / JPL mission planning, Mars synodic period 779.9 days

science.claim: The machine splits carbon dioxide (makes air).
science.working: Mars' air is about 95% CO2. NASA's MOXIE instrument on the Perseverance rover split Martian CO2 into oxygen electrochemically in 16 runs (2021-2023), making about 12 grams per hour, 122 grams in total.

Radar and spectrometer mapping (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter SHARAD, Odyssey GRS and neutron data) show water ice mixed into regolith a metre or less below the surface from the mid-latitudes poleward, in quantities that a mining-style dig could reach.
science.source: NASA MRO SHARAD subsurface radar; Odyssey GRS maps

science.working: Martian dust storms can cut arriving sunlight for weeks; on the 2018 global dust storm the solar-powered Opportunity rover stopped generating enough power and never recovered. Clearing dust off arrays is a real, routine duty on Mars.

shots.note: Pip at the bench by the window, lamp light, holds a chunk of blue ice; a shovel leans against the wall
the ice chunk on a metal tray under a heat lamp, dripping into the flask; the water level rises
the oxygen machine on the right: its gauge swings, the blinking lights go green one by one; Pip nods at it
Pip takes a long breath, relieved; the blue console light rims him
the storm beats on the window, the sun dims behind dust; Pip looks over from the bench
a monitor shows the solar array outside, crusted rust-red with dust; the output Gauge sits near zero
the wiper arm sweeps across the feed, the cleared band glints; the Gauge bar jumps
Pip throws the big breaker; the dome lamps come back on, the emergency strip dies; small in the frame
the habitat wide, Earth a pale dot in the darkening window; the title over it
two planets on their orbits, the transfer arc drawing on; 'ONE WINDOW' labels it
a 26-month counter runs up between the two orbit marks; the window blinks
Pip, worried; the console rim light starts to turn red
the storm swallows the window, the habitat lights sink to the red strip, the suit hangs ready; the last line lands
